newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris bourse bets on Suez /Lyonnaise merge.
newsitem.headline: Paris bourse bets on Suez /Lyonnaise merge.

text.p: A rumoured merger between holding company Cie de Suez and utilities group Lyonnaise des Eaux is viewed as probable, although Suez would need to change its structure beforehand, analysts said on Monday.
The two companies earlier declined comment on a British newspaper report which said they had appointed banks to advise them on the deal.
"The scheme is credible. Suez needs an industrial strategy. Lyonnaise needs funds to finance its expansion," said an analyst who asked not to be named.

Analysts believe Suez will need to make changes in its Societe Generale de Belgique (SGB) subsidiary, to take account of the Belgian authorities' hostility to a takeover of the Tractebel SA utilities firm by French investors.
One analyst who follows the sector said the market is looking for an offer of two Suez shares for every one Lyonnaise, to reflect the value of the shares on the market.
On Monday, Lyonnaise closed down 0.86 percent at 575 francs, while Suez was down 1.86 percent at 279.7. The market was off 2.16 percent.
If the merger went ahead, it would create a diversified group with almost 150 billion francs in annual turnover, active in services to local councils, television and financial services.
One analyst at a big French bank said Lyonnaise had total equity capital of 31 billion francs at the end of 1996 while debt stood at 22 billion francs.
"The group has a gearing of 73 percent. It is an acceptable level but it limits its expansion," he said.
Suez, meanwhile, had shareholders capital of 64 billion francs.

Suez owns nearly 17 percent of Lyonnaise's capital and around 21 percent of the voting rights. A merger between the two companies was raised in June 1995 by the then Suez chairman Gerard Worms to rival a plan to create a big French financial services group, linking insurer UAP and BNP bank, which would have taken over Suez.
That project did not come to fruition but analysts say a Suez-Lyonnaise merger could happen now, particularly as Lyonnaise chairman Jerome Monod is preparing for his retirement.
One possibility being voiced is that Monod could be chairman of the supervisory board of the new merged company, with Gerard Mestrallet, Suez chairman, taking the head of the executive committee.
The Belgian Prime minister Jean-Luc Dehaene and the Economics Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Elio di Rupo have said they are concerned about any merger as it could harm Belgian interests.
Suez owns 63 percent of SGB, which in turn controls Tractebel and Tractebel units, which have interests in energy, electricity production, gas distribution and waste management.

Lyonnaise's core activities are water contracts, construction, and energy. It also has the Lyonnaise Communications joint venture, which has stakes in the M6 television channel and TPS digital television service.

But besides the Belgian authorities, Suez' minority shareholders are also hostile to any merger, with the chairman of Cie Generale des Eaux (CGE), Jean-Marie Messier, warning that it would lead to a "strong dilution of earnings per share", in an interview with weekly newspaper, Investir.

CGE is Lyonnaise's main rival in France. Messier told Investir that a merger would mean minority shareholders who have supported Suez in its new strategy would not share in the rewards of that policy which had led to a strong cash position and ample liquid assets.
